verdicts.strongest_argument: The finding refutes itself in its own sentence: 'the stock absorbed it and closed 15.9% higher over the twenty sessions anyway.' That is the market considering the Google threat and declining to reprice DocuSign for it, which is the strongest form of already-priced available to me. The events are also wire copy stored in this capture - the Stocktwits news article on the Google Cloud AI release and the resulting 3% slide is at docs/61ddfe8b429fa05d4ddbc177c84432b69676ac6d.txt, indexed in snapshots/20260830T084004Z.json item 1, with entries dated 2026-08-26T04:36:16Z and 2026-08-22T01:08:24Z - so both the Workspace e-signature launch and the Cloud release were reported, headlined and dated a week or more before the print. Google entering e-signature is also a structural risk that has been on this name for years and appears in every DocuSign risk-factor section; a competitor's product launch that has been reported and traded is not new information three weeks later. What remains is a valuation assertion - that a terminal-value attack 'cannot be worth one 3% day' - with no dated source, no unit economics and no estimate of seat exposure, and it is the kind of claim that is unfalsifiable in either direction. The trendline and double-top corroboration is chart reading on the same bars. The 'no preview weighs the Google launch against the guide' argument is an n_queries=0 artefact of this capture.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Baseline: spot 65.97, run_up_20d +15.94%, run_up_5d +3.40%, pct_from_52w_low +58.01%. The twenty-session window that contains both Google headlines is the window in which the stock rose 16%. verdicts.what_would_change_it: A dated, quantified customer or seat datapoint - a churn disclosure, a named enterprise migration to Workspace signatures, a pricing concession - landing inside the July quarter rather than an inference about terminal value.

verdicts.strongest_argument: The hunter states the refutation itself: DocuSign insiders sell on standing plans every quarter, so the base rate is high and the marginal information is near zero. That is decisive and it is a size argument, not a publication argument - the filings are all in filings.json with dates, so they were reachable, but no body is stored and therefore not one share count or dollar value appears anywhere in this capture. Against a $12.18bn market cap and 3.16m shares a day of turnover, routine plan sales by executives are noise, and the July cluster of thirteen filings on 07-01 and 07-10 is exactly what scheduled post-print window openings look like at a company with broad equity compensation. A Form 4 also reports a completed transaction, so it describes supply already absorbed. I score it 32 rather than lower only because Form 144s genuinely are not surfaced by consumer aggregators and the capture does nothing to connect them.

verdicts.strongest_argument: This is a published consensus dataset, cited to the public web page that publishes it. estimize.com/docu/fq2-2027 is a free, indexed consensus site whose entire product is the spread between its crowd and the sell side, and the capture stores the page (docs/7fc221e837bcce8df517ae19d581b36a8f763c16.txt, snapshots/20260903T150816Z.json item 1). A number that a public consensus aggregator displays on its own landing page for the ticker on the morning of the print is the definition of already out - the anchors put 'restates published consensus' at the top of the scale. The size is also negligible: $0.04 on EPS and $6.98m on revenue against a quarterly revenue base of the order of three-quarters of a billion dollars is under one percent, well inside the noise of a name whose median reaction is 7.64%. The hunter's own framing concedes most of this - it signs the finding against its other two, calls Estimize a small self-selected crowd, and notes the same crowd skews bullish when retail is long, which makes the datum a sentiment reading rather than an estimate edge.
